questions.prompt: Water's formula is H₂O. What does this formula tell you about one water molecule?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Water's formula is H₂O, written as a capital H, a small 2, then a capital O. What does this formula tell you about one molecule of water?
questions.explanation: A formula is a parts list for one molecule. Each symbol names a kind of atom, and the small number written after a symbol says how many of those atoms there are; no number means one. So H₂O means every water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. The formula counts the atoms; it does not show how they are connected.

questions.hint: Which symbol is the small 2 written right after?

questions.explanation: All crystals repeat in three directions, but the repeating building block varies. Diamond and graphite repeat carbon atoms. questions.prompt: In this lesson's model, crystals and polymers are both extended structures. What is the main difference in how they repeat?
questions.accessiblePrompt: In this lesson's model, crystals and polymers are both extended structures. What is the main difference in how they repeat?
questions.explanation: Both are built by repeating a subunit, so neither has a set size. A crystal stacks its subunit, atoms or molecules, in a regular pattern in all three directions, like bricks in a wall that can grow every way. A polymer links its molecule-based units end to end in a long chain, like beads on a string.
questions.misconception: A polymer is just another word for a crystal, a polymer is a small molecule, or crystals and polymers differ by hardness.
questions.hint: Test each choice against examples you know, such as salt, ice, PVC and proteins.

scope.section: 3. Crystals and Polymers

evidence.supports: A crystal's atoms or molecules are arranged in repeating three-dimensional subunits.

choices.text: A polymer is one small molecule; a crystal is one giant molecule
choices.rationale: Neither is right: a polymer is a long chain of many units, and crystals such as salt are not molecules at all.

choices.text: Polymer units link into a chain; crystals repeat in all three directions
choices.rationale: Correct. A crystal stacks atoms or molecules in 3D, while a polymer strings molecule-based units into a long chain.

choices.text: Crystals have a set number of atoms, while polymers keep a constant ratio
choices.rationale: In the lesson's model, both repeat a subunit with no set size; what differs is the shape of the repetition.

choices.text: Crystals are always hard, and polymers are always soft and bendy
choices.rationale: Hardness isn't the dividing line: graphite is a soft crystal and PVC pipes are stiff polymers. The difference is the shape the repetition makes.

questions.limitations: Real polymer chains can coil, branch, or line up into partly orderly regions; the lesson's model keeps to simple chains.

questions.prompt: Graphite and diamond are both pure carbon. Why does the graphite in a pencil leave a gray line on paper when a diamond would not?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Graphite and diamond are both pure carbon. Why does the graphite in a pencil leave a gray line on paper when a diamond would not?
questions.explanation: Structure, not just composition, decides properties. In graphite, carbon atoms bond strongly within flat sheets of hexagons, but the sheets are only weakly held to one another, so friction peels thin layers onto the paper. In diamond, every carbon atom is bonded tightly to neighbors in all directions, so no layers can flake off.
questions.misconception: Pencil marks come from the metal lead, or different properties must mean different kinds of atoms.
questions.hint: Both are pure carbon, so the atoms themselves are identical. What else about them could be different?

evidence.supports: Graphite is thin sheets of carbon hexagons that scrape off onto paper; diamond's carbon atoms are held tightly in place, so no layer scrapes off.

evidence.title: Chemistry 2e, 10.5 The Solid State of Matter
evidence.supports: Graphite's planar sheets are held in layers by weak forces, so it is soft enough to be used as pencil lead and rubs off onto paper; diamond is hard because of strong bonding in all directions.

evidence.title: Pencils never contained lead
evidence.publisher: McGill University Office for Science and Society
evidence.supports: Pencil “lead” is a mixture of graphite and clay (more graphite makes a softer, darker point), and pencils have never contained lead metal.

choices.text: Pencils hold the metal lead, not carbon, so they mark paper.
choices.rationale: Despite the old name “pencil lead,” a pencil's core is graphite, a form of carbon, mixed with clay; it contains no lead metal.

choices.text: Diamond's carbon atoms are smaller than graphite's carbon atoms.
choices.rationale: Carbon atoms are carbon atoms. The difference is how they are bonded together, not their size.

choices.text: Graphite's sheets rub off; diamond's atoms are locked in place.
choices.rationale: Correct. Weakly stacked sheets slide off onto paper, while diamond's tightly bonded network holds every atom in place.

choices.text: Diamond is see-through, so any line it drew would be invisible.
choices.rationale: Color isn't the reason. Diamond's tightly held atoms don't scrape off, so it wouldn't leave a layer of carbon behind at all.

questions.prompt: An engineer needs a very hard edge for a saw blade that cuts steel. She can choose diamond or graphite. Based on their atomic structure, which should she pick?
questions.accessiblePrompt: An engineer needs a very hard edge for a saw blade that cuts steel. She can choose diamond or graphite. Based on their atomic structure, which should she pick?
questions.explanation: A cutting edge must be harder than the material it cuts. Diamond's carbon atoms are each bonded firmly to neighbors in every direction, making it one of the hardest materials known, so diamond-tipped blades can cut very hard materials, including steel. Graphite, with its weakly held layers, is soft.
questions.misconception: Two materials made of the same element will behave the same way, or being a crystal is by itself what makes a material hard.
questions.hint: Think about what a cutting edge must survive, and which structure could hold up.

scope.section: 4. Patterns You Can See

evidence.supports: Diamond's carbon atoms are held tightly in place, which makes diamonds good cutting tools for materials such as steel.

evidence.title: Chemistry 2e, 10.5 The Solid State of Matter
evidence.supports: Diamond is one of the hardest substances known because of strong bonding between carbon atoms in all directions; graphite is very soft.

evidence.title: Thermo-chemical wear model and worn tool shapes for single-crystal diamond tools cutting steel (Lane, Dow and Scattergood, Wear, 2013)
evidence.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
evidence.supports: The paper evaluates an Arrhenius-type (temperature-dependent) thermochemical wear model for predicting the wear of diamond tools when machining low carbon steel, and uses it to explain other researchers' results on the chemical wear of diamond.

evidence.publisher: Hokkaido University Collection of Scholarly and Academic Papers (HUSCAP)

choices.text: Graphite, because its sliding layers would give a smoother cut
choices.rationale: Layers that slide apart easily wear away quickly; that is why graphite rubs off onto paper. A cutting edge needs atoms that stay put.

choices.text: Either one, since both are made only of carbon
choices.rationale: Same element does not mean same properties. Graphite's sheets slide apart easily, which makes it soft, while diamond's firmly bonded network makes it extremely hard.

choices.text: Diamond, because its atoms are locked in a rigid 3D network
choices.rationale: Correct. Firm bonds in every direction make diamond extremely hard, which is what a cutting edge needs.

choices.text: Diamond, because it is a crystal and graphite is not
choices.rationale: Both are crystals of pure carbon. Being a crystal isn't what makes diamond hard; its atoms being bonded firmly in every direction is.

questions.prompt: Many snow crystals have six-fold symmetry, like six-armed stars or flat hexagons. What best explains this pattern?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Many snow crystals have six-fold symmetry: they look like six-armed stars or flat six-sided plates. What best explains this pattern?
questions.explanation: When water freezes, its molecules arrange in a repeating pattern built on hexagons. As a snow crystal grows, it copies that hidden pattern, so its faces and arms tend to show six-fold symmetry. Weather changes how the arms grow, which is why snow crystals vary and not every one is a perfect six-armed star.
questions.misconception: A visible shape like a hexagon must exist inside each individual particle.
questions.hint: The same six-fold pattern shows up in snow from many different storms. What could produce it every time?

choices.text: Wind trims the falling crystals into the same six-sided shapes.
choices.rationale: Wind tumbles snow crystals, but it couldn't carve the same symmetry again and again. The pattern comes from inside the crystal.

questions.limitations: Not every snow crystal is a perfect six-armed star; many form as columns, needles or irregular bits.

questions.prompt: Table salt grains tend to be tiny cubes. Suppose one grain is crushed into much smaller bits. Under a microscope, what would the bits most likely look like?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Table salt grains tend to be tiny cubes. Suppose one grain is crushed into much smaller bits. Under a microscope, what would the bits most likely look like?
questions.explanation: The cube-like pattern of sodium and chlorine runs through the whole grain, so salt tends to split along flat faces that meet at right angles. Crushing only makes the pieces smaller: each bit is still table salt, with sodium and chlorine in a 1:1 ratio and the same repeating pattern inside.
questions.misconception: Breaking a crystal into smaller pieces destroys its atomic pattern or separates its elements.
questions.hint: Does crushing change what the substance is, or only the size of the pieces?

scope.section: 3. Crystals and Polymers; Key Science Concept: Modeling Molecules and Extended Structures; 4. Patterns You Can See

evidence.supports: Grains of table salt seen under a microscope have a cube shape that reflects atomic-level structure.

evidence.locator: Key Science Concept: Modeling Molecules and Extended Structures
evidence.supports: A sodium chloride crystal can be very small or big because it is an extended structure, not molecules of a set size.
Salt's repeating subunit is sodium and chlorine atoms alternating to form a cube, in a 1:1 ratio.

evidence.title: 14.4: Halide Minerals (Mineralogy, Perkins et al.)
evidence.supports: Halite (rock salt) is a cubic mineral with pronounced cubic cleavage, so it breaks along flat faces at right angles; it also occurs in granular or massive forms and as hopper crystals.

choices.text: Smooth, round specks, because crushing wipes out the atom pattern
choices.rationale: Crushing makes the pieces smaller, but it can't rearrange the sodium and chlorine inside each piece; the pattern is still there.

choices.text: Smaller cube-like bits, since the pattern runs all through the grain
choices.rationale: Correct. The cube-like arrangement repeats through the whole grain, so salt tends to break along flat faces at right angles, giving smaller cube-like bits.

choices.text: Separate specks of pure sodium and specks of pure chlorine
choices.rationale: Crushing changes only the size. Each bit is still table salt, sodium and chlorine at 1:1, because an extended structure can be any size.

choices.text: Six-sided bits like snow crystals, since all crystals share that shape
choices.rationale: Each crystal's shape reflects its own pattern: salt's is cube-like, while ice's is built on hexagons.

questions.limitations: Crushed salt also has chipped, irregular bits; cube-like is a tendency, not a rule.

questions.prompt: Fewer than a hundred kinds of atoms occur naturally, yet Earth holds millions of different materials. Which idea from this lesson best explains how that is possible?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Fewer than a hundred kinds of atoms occur naturally, yet Earth holds millions of different materials. Which idea from this lesson best explains how that is possible?
questions.explanation: Atoms are like letters: a small set can be combined into a huge number of words. The same few kinds of atoms bond in different numbers (H₂O versus H₂O₂) and different arrangements (butane versus isobutane), and some repeat into crystals and polymers, so a short list of elements can build millions of materials.
questions.misconception: Each different material needs its own kind of atom.
questions.hint: Think about how a small set of letters can spell an enormous number of words.

scope.section: 1. Molecules and Chemical Bonds

evidence.supports: A small number of elements makes up millions of materials, much as a few letters make up all the words in a language: each element is one kind of atom, and atoms join through chemical bonds into more complex particles.

evidence.locator: Section 2. Composition and Structure of Molecules (Composition, Figure 2A)
evidence.supports: Water and hydrogen peroxide are made of the same two elements in different numbers, and they are different substances.

evidence.locator: Section 2. Composition and Structure of Molecules (Structure, Figure 2B)
evidence.supports: Butane and isobutane have the same atoms arranged differently, and they have different characteristics and uses.
Diamond and graphite are both made only of carbon, yet they are different materials.

choices.text: Atoms bond in different numbers and arrangements
choices.rationale: Correct. Like letters spelling many words, a few kinds of atoms combine in different counts (H₂O and H₂O₂) and different arrangements (butane and isobutane), and they can also repeat into crystals and polymers.

choices.text: Every material has its own special kind of atom
choices.rationale: Water and hydrogen peroxide are built from the same two kinds of atoms, and diamond and graphite are both only carbon, so different materials can share the same kinds of atoms.

choices.text: Atoms turn into new kinds of atoms as materials form
choices.rationale: Bonding joins atoms without changing which element they are: the hydrogen and oxygen atoms in water are still hydrogen and oxygen atoms.

choices.text: Each element's atoms come in many sizes and shapes
choices.rationale: In this lesson each element is made of one kind of atom. The variety comes from how atoms combine, not from many versions of each atom.

questions.prompt: An ice crystal is built from water molecules. When ice melts, its regular pattern breaks down, but every particle is still a whole water molecule. What does this suggest about what holds ice together?
questions.accessiblePrompt: An ice crystal is built from water molecules, each made of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. When ice melts, its regular pattern breaks down, but every particle is still a whole water molecule. What does this suggest about what holds ice together?
questions.explanation: Inside each water molecule, strong chemical bonds hold the two hydrogen atoms to the oxygen atom. In an ice crystal, weaker attractions between molecules keep them in a regular pattern. Melting needs only enough energy to loosen those weaker attractions, so the pattern breaks down while every molecule stays whole.
questions.misconception: Ice is held together by the same bonds that hold each water molecule together, so melting must break water molecules apart.
questions.hint: Look closely at what melting changed and what it left the same.

scope.section: 3. Crystals and Polymers; Key Science Concept: Modeling Molecules and Extended Structures

evidence.supports: In a crystal made of molecules, strong chemical bonds hold the atoms inside each molecule together, while other attractions hold the molecules to one another; water forms such a crystal, ice, when it freezes.

evidence.locator: Key Science Concept: Modeling Molecules and Extended Structures
evidence.supports: Ice is a crystal of water molecules.

evidence.title: Chemistry 2e, 10.1 Intermolecular Forces
evidence.supports: Attractions between small molecules are usually weak compared with the bonds inside them, and intramolecular forces keep a molecule intact; for example, breaking the bonds inside one mole of HCl takes about 25 times more energy than overcoming the attractions between its molecules to boil it.

choices.text: The bonds inside each molecule are stronger than the attractions between molecules
choices.rationale: Correct. Melting loosens the attractions between molecules but leaves the bonds inside each molecule unbroken, so the bonds inside must be the stronger ones.

choices.text: The attractions between molecules are stronger than the bonds inside each molecule
choices.rationale: If that were so, melting would split the molecules apart before freeing them from one another. The opposite happens: every molecule stays whole.

choices.text: Ice is one giant molecule, held together by the same kind of bond throughout
choices.rationale: Ice is a crystal of many separate water molecules. Melting frees them from their places but leaves each one whole, so the attractions between molecules must be a different, weaker kind of link.

choices.text: Nothing holds the molecules; they simply rest against one another
choices.rationale: Then ice could not hold a solid shape. Attractions between the molecules keep them locked in the crystal's regular pattern.

questions.limitations: Liquid water still has attractions between its molecules; melting loosens the ice pattern rather than freeing every molecule completely. The item compares only bonds inside molecules with attractions between them.
